event_title: Crude oil spike on Hormuz escalation, hot June WPI and rupee past 96 pressure Indian equities
summary: Renewed US-Iran hostilities over the Strait of Hormuz drove Brent up 14% over four sessions to $85.6/bbl, roughly 19% above its early-July low of about $72; a separate report put Brent at $86.85 on 15 July, so the two sources describe the same mid-$80s move on different bases rather than confirming a single print. Alongside this, June wholesale inflation came in at 9.87% with fuel and power at 27.41%, and the rupee breached 96 per dollar. Foreign portfolio investors reversed an eight-session buying streak to sell Rs 7,443 crore over four sessions, and the Sensex and Nifty closed 0.72% and 0.66% lower on 15 July.

chain.mechanism: About a fifth of global oil supplies transit the Strait of Hormuz, so a contested or blockaded waterway puts an outsized share of seaborne supply at risk
Threatened supply attracts a risk premium into the benchmark: Brent climbed 14% over four sessions to $85.6 and is roughly 19% above its early-July low of about $72

terminal_impact.conditionality: if Hormuz access remains contested and the interim US-Iran agreement stays unresolved

chain.mechanism: India meets the large majority of its crude demand through imports (approximately 85%*), so a higher benchmark price raises the dollar import bill close to proportionally. No supplied fact states India's import-dependency share, so this hop carries no citation
A larger oil import bill widens the current-account deficit and structural dollar demand, adding depreciation pressure; the rupee has breached the 96-per-dollar mark

A weaker rupee erodes dollar-denominated returns for foreign investors, who are described as viewing India largely through the prism of oil prices; FPIs turned net sellers of Rs 7,443 crore over four sessions including Rs 4,206 crore in the latest session

Sustained FPI selling withdraws marginal demand from the large-cap benchmarks foreign investors are most concentrated in; the benchmark indices closed lower on 15 July, with CY2026 cumulative outflows of Rs 2.6 trillion already exceeding any prior full calendar year

terminal_impact.conditionality: if Brent sustains above roughly $90 and FPI selling persists beyond a few sessions

chain.mechanism: Crude feeds directly into mineral oils and the fuel-and-power wholesale group; mineral oils inflation ran at 46.48% and crude petroleum and natural gas at 34.75% in June, with fuel and power at 27.41%
Fuel and power is a major WPI group, so elevated fuel prices hold headline wholesale inflation up; the all-commodities index rose to 110.2 and headline WPI to 9.87% in June
Persistently high wholesale inflation narrows the room for policy easing. No fact on the RBI's stance or reaction function was supplied, so this hop is reasoning only

terminal_impact.conditionality: if crude-driven inflation carries into the next policy review

investor_actions_conditional.if: Brent sustains above roughly $90 for several weeks
investor_actions_conditional.then: upstream and energy exposure behaves as a partial natural hedge against the import-bill channel, while aviation and paints exposure carries the opposite input-cost sensitivity and is worth reviewing

investor_actions_conditional.if: FPI selling continues alongside a weaker rupee
investor_actions_conditional.then: large-cap indices with the heaviest foreign ownership are more exposed to the flow channel than domestically-owned mid and small caps
the relative pull of developed-market bonds remains a second headwind to FPI return that is independent of crude, so a crude retreat alone may not restore inflows

rm_one_liner: This is largely an oil story: a Hormuz-driven crude spike is feeding inflation, weakening the rupee and pushing foreign investors to sell, which pressures large-cap indices until crude and the West Asia situation settle.
